reasoning: Long oo in the first syllable. Literally oats, and used for the cooked porridge as well, so the English holds.
أكثر is said aktar with t in Palestinian, and ishi for thing is specifically Palestinian against Syrian shi. Word-initial hamza seats are not romanized.
ظ is written TH per the scheme; many Ramallah speakers realise it as an emphatic z here. Taa marbuta after ف is e.
English loan, both syllables with long aa plus a final y glide. Universal in Ramallah speech.
Form II participle with the initial m- unvowelled, and a shadda doubling the waw. Feminine mlawwane.
Shadda on the ر, so a doubled r, then a long ii. Also used as a noun for the villain in a film.
Long aa then a final ii: haadi, of a person or a place. Feminine haadye.
خ is a moon letter so the article stays il-. ق is a glottal stop and both ط are emphatic; the b- present gives habitual or repeated action.

meaning_fix: wasted his effort / got nowhere (lit: pounded water and it stayed water)
reasoning: The idiom is about futile effort rather than evading a question, which is what beating around the bush means. The usual Levantine shapes are دق مي بمي or اللي بدق المي مي بتضل, so this wording is clipped and I am unsure of the intended reading.
il- assimilates to the sun letter س. kharbaan is the everyday Palestinian word for out of order, feminine kharbaane with e after ن.
Turkish loan said with long oo and a final e after ب. Standard in Ramallah kitchens.
yoom has a long oo. Hamza after the article is not written because the article vowel runs straight into it: il-a7ad.
Quadriliteral participle with ق as a glottal stop and an unvowelled initial m-. Used of crisps, biscuits and fried food.
Imperative with the initial cluster tw-, and in fast speech 3ala allah runs together as 3a-llah. Said to push someone to get started.
The taa marbuta of مكنسة surfaces as t in the construct, so it is respelled with a plain ت for the voice. Ramallah speakers also say miknase kahrabaa'iyye.
A collective noun, pears as a kind, with ص as emphatic S. Often heard with a helping vowel as injaaS.
bi plus the article assimilating to the sun letter ت gives bit-. Final ق is a glottal stop in this everyday send-off.
ه does not block the raising of taa marbuta, so e, though jabha is also heard. The same word means a front in the political or military sense.
Long ee, not ii: 3eele, the colloquial form of عائلة. Taa marbuta after ل is e.
Shadda on the ي gives the doubled yy before the final e. Short for ma7miyye Tabii3iyye, a protected natural area.
b- present of ظنّ with a doubled final n, and la' for no with a final glottal stop. A Ramallah speaker might equally say ma baTHunn.
Both ب and ق are moon letters, so the article stays il- twice, and ق is a glottal stop. Of Jerusalem or Nablus, people often just say il-balad.
Emphatic ط and a glottal ق. The possessive is -o in Palestinian, 3a'lo not 3a'luh.
Form II participle, shadda doubling the ر, initial m- unvowelled. Used both of an old person rambling and of anyone talking rubbish.
Past tense you-m. with the initial cluster fh-, and علي here is 3alayy with a doubled y, me rather than him. The question mark is not romanized.
